title: The Nudge of Thanking People in Advance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post opens with a run of behavioral-science examples of nudges, from an eye image deterring bicycle theft to a stairs sign nearly doubling stair use, to set up its main idea: environmental cues and priming can shape workplace behavior. The author's specific proposal is for leaders to thank people in advance for conduct they hope to see, an idea credited to Ben Franklin. Examples include thanking a group for keeping the fridge clean or for their commitment to a new sales process. The author argues this is effective and not manipulative, since it reinforces what people already intend, and singles out three high-value uses: appreciation for quality work before it is done, for candor before it happens, and for following norms before they are followed.
points: Small environmental cues and priming statements can raise compliance without coercion, and leaders can use them deliberately.
Thanking people in advance signals the norm the leader expects and invites people to live up to it.
The three most useful advance thanks concern quality work, candor and adherence to group norms.
The author frames the technique as reinforcing existing intentions, which is why it is not underhanded.
quotes: These so-called nudges rely on cues placed in the environment to subtly influence behavior. Specific words, photos, and music prime people to do things they would likely do anyway, but they reinforce the need to do them. Such nudges and priming messages are powerful tools for gaining higher compliance in the workplace.

Ben Franklin understood nudges all too well. He was perhaps the first to write about the power of thanking people in advance for work that has yet to be done. The nudge of thanking people in advance for gaining compliance and commitment is highly effective and not in the least bit underhanded.
A simple, “Thanks to everyone who has cleaned out the company refrigerator,” encourages people to keep the fridge free of old food and points to a norm a leader wants to reaffirm.
Thanking people in advance for something they would do anyway is simply a nudge and nothing more. But it works.

Consider incorporating these nudges in your everyday leadership. You might find that team members live up to the expectations that you set. Sometimes people just need a little nudge to do what they always intended to.
